title: Braised Oxtail
subtitle: Oxtail slow-braised in red wine and beef stock until falling from the bone
excerpt: Braised oxtail is one of the great British long-cook dishes: oxtail pieces browned hard, then braised in red wine and beef stock for three hours until the meat collapses from the bone into a deeply gelatinous gravy. It takes most of a day but almost none of that time is active cooking.
sourceNotes: Oxtail as a braising cut has a long history in British and European cooking, where nothing from the animal was wasted. The high collagen content of the tail produces a sticky, rich gravy as it cooks that no other cut can match.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze after the braise and cooling. Defrost overnight and reheat gently, uncovered, in a low oven at 150°C fan for 45 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Braise the day before and refrigerate. The fat solidifies overnight and can be scraped off before reheating. The flavour improves significantly.

glossaryTerms.definition: A slow-cooking method where food is browned first in fat, then cooked in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot. The long, moist heat breaks down connective tissue into gelatin, which thickens the sauce.

content.text: oxtail rewards patience. The initial browning of the oxtail is the most important step: get good colour on all sides before adding any liquid. The long braise (three to three-and-a-half hours in a low oven) melts the collagen from the bone into the gravy and makes the meat pull free without effort. Oxtail is done when it slides off the bone at a touch.

items.prepNote: jointed into sections, excess fat trimmed

content.text: Heat the oven to 150°C fan. Pat the oxtail sections dry and season generously with salt and pepper. Heat a little oil in a large Dutch oven over high heat. Brown the oxtail in batches, getting good colour on all sides (3 to 4 minutes per batch). Do not crowd the pan. Set browned pieces aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add {{onion}} chopped onion, {{carrot}} chopped carrot, and {{celery}} chopped celery. Cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic and {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring.

Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes to burn off the alcohol. Return the oxtail to the pot. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, the thyme, and the bay leaves. The liquid should come about three-quarters of the way up the oxtail.

Bring to a simmer, cover tightly, and transfer to the oven. Braise for 3 to 3.5 hours until the meat falls from the bone at a gentle push. Turn the pieces halfway through if they are not fully submerged.

Lift out the oxtail pieces. Strain the braising liquid into a clean pan and skim off the fat. Reduce over high heat until glossy and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Taste and season. Return the oxtail to the sauce.

items.symptom: The meat is still tough after 3 hours
items.cause: Oxtail can be very variable in age and size. A larger, older animal takes longer.
items.fix: Cover and return to the oven for a further 45 minutes. It is done when the meat pulls free from the bone without resistance.

items.symptom: The gravy is thin and watery
items.cause: The oxtail was not browned properly or the braising liquid was too much.
items.fix: Reduce the strained braising liquid over high heat until it coats a spoon thickly. Oxtail releases gelatin as it cooks, so the sauce should thicken naturally.

items.symptom: The oxtail has a strong, gamey flavour
items.cause: The fat was not trimmed before cooking or the oxtail was not browned in batches.
items.fix: Trim the excess hard fat before cooking. Good browning at the start also reduces any off-notes by developing the flavour of the meat.

items.cause: Oxtail is a fatty cut; the fat separates during braising.
items.fix: Skim the surface of the braising liquid thoroughly after straining. For the cleanest result, chill overnight and remove the solidified fat layer before reheating.

content.text: Oxtail has been a prized cut in British cooking since at least the eighteenth century. It was sold as street food in London and used throughout working-class kitchens. It went out of fashion as cheaper cuts became common, but returned to restaurant menus in the 1990s when nose-to-tail cooking came back into favour. Serve with creamy mash, braised red cabbage, or buttered egg noodles.
